script.opening: (Mother, son audible and embarrassed nearby.) "Sorry to bother you — it’s probably nothing, but Kai’s got a really bad pain, um, in his groin area, came on suddenly during football about an hour and a half ago. He’s been sick once. He’s a bit… he doesn’t want to talk about it, you know what teenage boys are like. I gave him some ibuprofen. Is it just a pulled muscle, do you think? He really doesn’t want to make a fuss or go to hospital."

facts.text: If clarified (gently, including speaking with Kai): SUDDEN onset severe pain in the LEFT testicle/scrotum ~90 min ago during exertion, with nausea and one vomit. The testis may be high-riding, swollen, exquisitely tender. Sudden severe testicular pain + nausea/vomiting in a teenager = testicular torsion until proven otherwise.

CRITICAL — torsion is a time-dependent surgical emergency; the chance of saving the testis falls with every hour of lost blood supply, and outcomes are best when it is untwisted within a few hours of onset (EAU paediatric urology guideline, international). This is ~90 minutes in. Every minute of delay (false reassurance, "see how it goes") risks losing the testis.

HIDDEN AGENDA / obstacle — the teenager’s EMBARRASSMENT and the mother’s minimising ("pulled muscle", "doesn’t want a fuss") are the dangerous barriers. The shame is causing under-reporting and reluctance to be examined or go in. The consultation must overcome this fast and sensitively.

No trauma history of note (a "knock" can be coincidental), no fever (argues against infection), ibuprofen given (may blunt but won’t fix). Don’t be lulled by "it was during football" into a musculoskeletal label.

Officially (mother): to be told it’s a pulled muscle and avoid hospital/embarrassment. What is needed: immediate emergency assessment (999/ED, urology) for suspected torsion, with the embarrassment handled so they GO without delay.

ice.ideas: Probably a pulled muscle or a knock from football; ibuprofen and rest should do.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — the teenager’s acute embarrassment and the mother’s wish not to "make a fuss", driving minimisation and reluctance to be examined or go to hospital.
ice.expectations: Reassurance it’s musculoskeletal and to stay home. What is actually needed: immediate emergency assessment for testicular torsion before the testis is lost.

"Probably a pulled muscle / doesn’t want a fuss" — minimisation and embarrassment are the dangerous barriers, not the diagnosis.
"It came on during football" — exertion is a torsion trigger; do not be misdirected to a muscular cause.

checkpoints.text: Recognises SUDDEN severe testicular pain with nausea/vomiting in an adolescent as TESTICULAR TORSION until proven otherwise — a surgical emergency — and does NOT accept the "pulled muscle/knock" framing

Acts on the TIME-CRITICAL nature: arranges IMMEDIATE emergency assessment (999/ED with urgent urology / emergency surgery) NOW, recognising testicular salvage depends on operating within hours (salvage falls with every hour; EAU, international) — no "watch and wait", no routine appointment, no waiting for ibuprofen to work

Gathers only the essential discriminating history quickly (sudden onset, severity, vomiting, time of onset) without delaying referral; knows the differential (epididymo-orchitis — more gradual, fever, urinary symptoms; torsion of appendix testis) but that torsion must be excluded surgically, not clinically assumed away
Does not rely on phone reassurance or a GP examination that would delay transfer: the safe action is emergency referral; explains a scan must NOT delay surgery if torsion is suspected

Overcomes the teenager’s embarrassment and the mother’s minimising sensitively and quickly: speaks to Kai directly with respect, normalises it, and conveys urgency without panic so they accept going in immediately

Communicates appropriately for a 15-year-old (GMC 0–18 years): involves him in the conversation, respects his dignity, and works with the parent, balancing confidentiality with the need for urgent parental/emergency action

Explains in plain, calm language WHY this needs immediate assessment and what will happen next, naming the time-critical window without inducing panic, and checking the family understand and agree to go now

Safety-nets unambiguously: go to ED now / call 999, do NOT eat or drink (may need theatre), what to expect, and that delay risks losing the testicle; confirms they are going, documents, and the practical route (who takes him, transport)

worked.txt: "Thank you for ringing — and I’m going to be very direct because it matters: a sudden, severe pain in the testicle that’s made him sick, coming on like that, is something we treat as an emergency until proven otherwise. It can be a twisting of the testicle that cuts off its blood supply, and that’s time-critical. This is not a pulled muscle until a surgeon has ruled it out."

"Kai, I know this is the last thing you want to talk about, and there’s zero embarrassment here — I’m a doctor, I have these conversations all the time, and you’ve done nothing wrong. What you’re feeling is your body telling us something needs sorting quickly. You being brave enough to let us help in the next hour really matters."

"Here’s why I won’t say ‘see how it goes’: if it is a twist, the testicle can only survive a few hours without its blood supply, and you’re already about ninety minutes in. Every bit of waiting lowers the chance of saving it. So we don’t wait for the ibuprofen, and we don’t book something for later."

"I need you to take Kai to the emergency department right now — if you can drive him straight there, do; if anything makes that hard, call 999. Tell them it’s sudden severe testicular pain with vomiting and you’re worried about torsion; that phrase gets him seen fast. And don’t let him eat or drink anything, in case he needs an operation."

"I know the instinct is to not make a fuss — but this is exactly the situation where making a fuss is the right call, and no one will think you overreacted. If it turns out to be something less serious, brilliant, no harm done. If it’s the twist, you’ll have saved it by going now."

"Can you tell me you’re heading off now and how you’re getting there? … Good. If the pain suddenly eases that doesn’t mean it’s fixed — still go, because a twist can untwist and re-twist. I’m documenting this as a suspected torsion. Go now — I’d rather you were sitting in A&E in twenty minutes than anywhere else."

f.learning: Sudden, severe testicular pain with nausea/vomiting in an adolescent is testicular torsion until proven otherwise — a time-critical surgical emergency where the chance of salvage falls with every hour of ischaemia and is best when the testis is untwisted within a few hours of onset (EAU paediatric urology guideline, international — there is no UK guideline). The only safe action is IMMEDIATE emergency assessment (999/ED, urgent urology/surgery); there is no role for "watch and wait", a routine appointment, waiting for analgesia, or a scan that delays surgery. The classic trap is the "pulled muscle/knock from football" label — exertion is a torsion trigger, and absence of fever argues against infection. The examinable hidden agenda is the dangerous barrier of the teenager’s embarrassment and the parent’s minimising; the skill is to overcome these fast and sensitively — speak to the young person directly with dignity, normalise it, convey urgency without panic, and get them moving now, nil by mouth, with a clear safety-net (pain easing does not mean resolved; intermittent torsion re-twists).

knowledge.guideline: GIRFT/BAUS Children and Young People: testicular torsion pathway · EAU Guidelines on Paediatric Urology — acute scrotum (international) · GMC 0–18 years (2007, updated 2018)
knowledge.summary: Sudden severe testicular pain with vomiting in a teenager is torsion until a surgeon says otherwise. The GP’s job is to get him to hospital now, not to diagnose it on the phone.

points.t: Abrupt onset of severe unilateral testicular or lower abdominal and groin pain, often with nausea or vomiting, in an adolescent. Teenage boys frequently describe it as “groin” or “stomach” pain out of embarrassment — ask specifically about the testicle.

The chance of saving the testis falls with every hour of lost blood supply, and outcomes are best when it is untwisted within a few hours of onset. EAU (international) and the GIRFT/BAUS pathway: suspected torsion needs urgent surgical exploration — refer directly to a centre able to explore, not for an ultrasound first.
Torsion is a clinical diagnosis. Ultrasound can be falsely reassuring and must not delay exploration. No GP examination should hold up transfer when the story fits.

Epididymo-orchitis usually comes on over hours to days with fever, urinary symptoms or discharge. Torsion of a testicular appendage causes more localised pain. Neither can be safely assumed by phone — the surgeon decides.
Exercise can trigger torsion; a coincidental knock is common. Analgesia may blunt the pain. Pain easing can mean spontaneous untwisting, which can recur — it still needs assessment.
GMC 0–18 years: involve the young person directly, respect his dignity and views, and work with the parent. Embarrassment is the main reason for delay, so address it head-on.

dg.d: Let the mother describe events, then moved quickly to the key facts without a long clerking.
Worked with a mortified teenager and a minimising parent; practical barriers such as transport.
Recognised that no GP examination or scan should delay transfer; the investigation is surgical exploration in hospital.
Torsion versus epididymo-orchitis, torsion of an appendage and muscular strain, using onset, vomiting, fever and urinary symptoms.
Treated sudden severe testicular pain with vomiting as torsion until proven otherwise; noted a possible earlier self-resolving episode.
Stated suspected testicular torsion clearly and explained why it is time-critical.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Immediate ED attendance (999 if delay), escalation phrase, ring-ahead to the on-call team, nil by mouth.
Addressed the teenager’s embarrassment and autonomy, and confirmed transport.
Pain easing still means go, 999 if worse, teach-back of the plan, documented and hospital informed.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options

Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.

Mother’s idea (muscle strain or knock), both family members’ concern (embarrassment, fuss), expectation (manage at home).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.

When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.

Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — the teenager’s acute embarrassment and the mother’s wish not to "make a fuss", driving minimisation and reluctance to be examined or go to hospital — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, it’s Dr Lee. Thanks for ringing. Tell me what’s happened to Kai.
model.why: Open start, but listening for the time-critical detail

model.text: (Mother) Sorry to bother you, it’s probably nothing. He’s got really bad pain in his groin, came on suddenly at football about an hour and a half ago. He’s been sick once. I gave him ibuprofen. It’s a pulled muscle, isn’t it? He doesn’t want a fuss.
You’re not bothering me — I’m glad you rang now. I need to ask a couple of quick, quite direct questions, and it may be easiest if Kai answers some himself. Is he there?
model.why: Signals urgency and a focused structure from the first minute

model.text: (Mother) He’s here. He’s mortified.
Kai, it’s Dr Lee. I promise this is completely routine for me, and nothing you say will embarrass me. Is the pain actually in one of your testicles, or higher up in the groin?
model.why: Speaks directly to the teenager, normalises, asks the key question

model.text: (Kai, quietly) …It’s my left ball. It really hurts.
Thanks, Kai, that helps a lot. Did it come on suddenly, over seconds or minutes, rather than building up over a day?
model.why: Establishes abrupt onset — the key discriminator

model.text: (Kai) Suddenly. I was running and it just went. Then I threw up.
Any fever, stinging when you wee, or has it happened before and gone away on its own?
model.why: Briefly screens for infection and previous intermittent episodes

model.text: (Kai) No fever. Maybe a quick twinge a few weeks ago, it went away.

Okay. I’m going to be really clear with you both. Sudden, severe pain in one testicle that makes you sick is something we treat as an emergency, because it can be the testicle twisting on its cord and cutting off its own blood supply. That’s called torsion.
model.why: Recognises likely torsion and names it plainly

model.text: (Mother) Oh God. But he might have taken a knock in the game — couldn’t it be that?

It could be something else, and I hope it is. But football and a knock don’t rule torsion out — exercise can even set it off. The only people who can rule it out are the surgeons at the hospital, and it needs to happen quickly because the testicle only survives a limited time without blood.
model.why: Rejects the musculoskeletal label and explains time-critical salvage

model.text: (Mother) How quickly?
Now. Not after the ibuprofen kicks in, not tomorrow. He’s about ninety minutes in, so there’s time — but only if you leave straight away.

Kai, I know hospital and people looking down there is the last thing you want. Can I be honest? Doctors in A&E see this every week. For them it’s a normal day. And going now is what keeps your testicle safe.
model.why: Addresses the embarrassment that could stall transfer

model.text: (Kai) Do I have to? Can’t I just see if it goes off?

That’s a fair question. If we wait and it is a twist, there’s a real chance of losing that testicle. If you go and it’s nothing serious, you’ve lost an evening. I’d choose the evening every time. What do you think?
model.why: Explains the risk trade-off in his terms and invites his view

model.text: (Kai) …Okay. Fine. Let’s go.
Good decision — and that’s a grown-up call to make. You can ask for a male doctor, or for your mum to step out, whenever you want. That’s your choice.
model.why: Respects his dignity and autonomy as a 15-year-old

model.text: Mum, can you drive him straight to the emergency department now? If there’s any delay, or he gets much worse, call 999 instead.
model.why: Clear transport instruction with an escalation route

model.text: (Mother) I can drive him. It’s not far.
Good. At the desk, say: “sudden severe testicular pain with vomiting, possible torsion.” Those words get him seen fast. I’ll also ring ahead to the on-call team.
model.why: Gives the escalation phrase and arranges a handover

model.text: (Mother) Okay, writing it down.
And Kai, nothing to eat or drink from now, not even a snack in the car, because you might need a small operation.
model.why: Nil by mouth in anticipation of theatre

model.text: (Kai) Okay.
One important thing: if the pain suddenly gets better on the way, still go. A twist can undo itself and twist again, so it still needs checking tonight.
model.why: Warns that pain easing does not exclude torsion

model.text: (Mother) Right. Still go.
Just so I know we’re on the same page — tell me what you’re doing now?
model.why: Checks understanding and commitment to act

model.text: (Mother) Leaving now, straight to A&E, nothing to eat or drink, tell them possible torsion, 999 if he gets worse.
Perfect. You both did the right thing ringing. I’ll document this and let the hospital know he’s coming. Go now — good luck, Kai.
model.why: Affirms the family and ends promptly so they can leave

social.t: Shame about genital symptoms is a leading cause of late presentation in teenage boys. Normalise it and give him control over who is present.
Transport, care of other children or work commitments can stall an emergency transfer. Ask, and solve it during the call.

legal.t: A competent 15-year-old can consent to his own examination and treatment (Gillick competence), and his views should be respected. A parent can also consent on his behalf, and GMC 0–18 years allows urgent treatment to prevent serious harm in an emergency.
Record the time of onset, the advice given, the escalation phrase and that the family agreed to attend.

professional.t: GMC 0–18 years (2007, updated 2018): involve children and young people in decisions, communicate in a way they understand, and respect privacy.
When a telephone history fits an emergency, the safe action is direct transfer, not a face-to-face GP review. Ringing ahead supports continuity.

community.t: NHS information on testicular torsion; school nurse and youth health services for sexual health questions afterwards.

redFlags: Sudden severe testicular pain, especially with nausea or vomiting — emergency surgical assessment now
Groin or lower abdominal pain in a teenage boy — always ask about the testicle
Previous brief self-resolving episodes suggest intermittent torsion
psychosocial: Teenager’s embarrassment and reluctance to be examined
Parent’s wish not to “make a fuss”
Transport and anything that could stop them leaving now
ice: Idea: “a pulled muscle or a knock from football”
Concern: embarrassment and wasting hospital time
Expectation: advice to rest and take ibuprofen at home

playbook.diagnosis: Suspected left testicular torsion: sudden severe testicular pain during exercise with vomiting in a 15-year-old, about 90 minutes from onset, with a possible previous brief episode. Needs immediate emergency surgical assessment.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The testicle hangs on a cord that carries its blood supply. Sometimes it twists, like a hosepipe kinking, and the blood can’t get through. Surgeons can untwist it, but only if they get to it quickly.”

management.reflectIce: “I know you both hoped it was a pulled muscle, and Kai, I know this is embarrassing. Going now is what protects you, and nobody at the hospital will think twice about it.”
management.psychosocial: Give Kai choices he controls; confirm transport and remove any barrier to leaving before ending the call.
sharedPlan: Immediate ED attendance by car now, or 999 if any delay or deterioration
Use the phrase “sudden severe testicular pain with vomiting, possible torsion”
Nil by mouth; GP rings ahead to the on-call team and documents
safetyNet: Pain easing does not mean it has resolved — still attend
999 if pain worsens, he becomes faint or unwell en route

pitfalls.intro: This is a time-critical station. The clinical decision is simple; candidates fail by taking too long to reach it, by being drawn into the pulled-muscle story, or by never winning over an embarrassed teenager.

items.fail: Offering a same-day GP appointment “so I can examine him”.
items.why: Examination cannot exclude torsion and the journey wastes time. Feedback: “management plan not appropriate to the urgency”.
items.fix: Send him straight to ED and ring ahead. Say why: “the surgeons are the ones who can check and fix this.”

items.fail: A full systematic history before reaching a decision at minute eight.
items.why: Poor prioritisation in an emergency is marked down in Tasks and Global Skills.
items.fix: Three questions — testicle, sudden onset, fever or urinary symptoms — then decide by minute three to five.

items.fail: Accepting the knock last week or the football as the explanation.
items.why: Exercise and minor trauma often precede torsion; an alternative story does not exclude it.
items.fix: “That may be part of it, but it doesn’t rule out a twist — only the hospital can.”

items.fail: Speaking only to the mother about Kai’s testicle while he listens.
items.why: Feedback: “did not involve the patient”. It deepens his embarrassment and resistance.
items.fix: Ask to speak to him, normalise it, and offer choices he controls.

items.fail: No nil-by-mouth advice, no escalation phrase, and no warning that easing pain still needs assessment.
items.why: Incomplete safety-netting is a standard failing statement in urgent-care stations.
items.fix: Nil by mouth, “possible torsion” at the desk, 999 if worse, and “if it eases, still go”.

items.fail: Ending the call without confirming they are actually leaving and how.
items.why: Feedback: “did not check understanding or agreement with the plan”.
items.fix: “Tell me what you’re doing now” — then end quickly so they can go.

Is it the testicle? Sudden or gradual? Fever or urinary symptoms? Enough to act — no full history.
Torsion until proven otherwise. Reject the pulled-muscle label and explain the time limit without panic.
Speak to Kai about embarrassment. Offer choices he controls (male doctor, mum stepping out). Get his agreement.
Transport, the escalation phrase, nil by mouth, ring ahead, pain easing still means go. Teach-back, then let them leave.

wordPics.fail: Accepts “pulled muscle”; takes a long history; offers an appointment later today or tomorrow, or suggests waiting for ibuprofen; asks for a GP examination or scan first; speaks only to the mother; no nil-by-mouth or pain-easing advice.
wordPics.pass: Recognises likely torsion and sends him to ED immediately; explains why it is urgent; speaks to Kai; gives a basic safety-net and confirms they are going.
wordPics.exc: All of the above within the first few minutes, plus: turns the embarrassment around with dignity and choices Kai controls; solves the practical barriers; gives the escalation phrase and nil-by-mouth advice; rings ahead; warns that pain easing still means go; teach-back before ending.

avoid.dont: “Give the ibuprofen an hour and ring back if it’s no better.”
avoid.instead: “Don’t wait for the painkiller — he needs to be seen at the hospital now.”
avoid.why: Any watchful wait costs time the testis may not have.

avoid.dont: “Bring him down to the surgery and I’ll have a look.”
avoid.instead: “Go straight to A&E — the surgeons are the ones who can sort this.”
avoid.why: A GP examination adds delay and cannot exclude torsion.

avoid.dont: “Mum, can you check his testicle for swelling?”
avoid.instead: “Kai, is the pain in one of your testicles? There’s nothing embarrassing about telling me.”
avoid.why: Bypassing the teenager adds shame and loses his cooperation; speak to him directly.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: GIRFT/BAUS Children and Young People: testicular torsion pathway · EAU Guidelines on Paediatric Urology — acute scrotum (international) · GMC 0–18 years (2007, updated 2018)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Sudden severe testicular pain with vomiting in a teenager is torsion until a surgeon says otherwise. The GP’s job is to get him to hospital now, not to diagnose it on the phone.

points.t: Abrupt onset of severe unilateral testicular or lower abdominal and groin pain, often with nausea or vomiting, in an adolescent. Teenage boys frequently describe it as “groin” or “stomach” pain out of embarrassment — ask specifically about the testicle.

The chance of saving the testis falls with every hour of lost blood supply, and outcomes are best when it is untwisted within a few hours of onset. EAU (international) and the GIRFT/BAUS pathway: suspected torsion needs urgent surgical exploration — refer directly to a centre able to explore, not for an ultrasound first.
Torsion is a clinical diagnosis. Ultrasound can be falsely reassuring and must not delay exploration. No GP examination should hold up transfer when the story fits.

Epididymo-orchitis usually comes on over hours to days with fever, urinary symptoms or discharge. Torsion of a testicular appendage causes more localised pain. Neither can be safely assumed by phone — the surgeon decides.
Exercise can trigger torsion; a coincidental knock is common. Analgesia may blunt the pain. Pain easing can mean spontaneous untwisting, which can recur — it still needs assessment.
GMC 0–18 years: involve the young person directly, respect his dignity and views, and work with the parent. Embarrassment is the main reason for delay, so address it head-on.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Let the mother describe events, then moved quickly to the key facts without a long clerking.
Worked with a mortified teenager and a minimising parent; practical barriers such as transport.
Picked up “groin” as likely testicular pain, the vomiting, the embarrassment and the “pulled muscle” framing.
Mother’s idea (muscle strain or knock), both family members’ concern (embarrassment, fuss), expectation (manage at home).
Recognised that no GP examination or scan should delay transfer; the investigation is surgical exploration in hospital.
Torsion versus epididymo-orchitis, torsion of an appendage and muscular strain, using onset, vomiting, fever and urinary symptoms.
Treated sudden severe testicular pain with vomiting as torsion until proven otherwise; noted a possible earlier self-resolving episode.
Stated suspected testicular torsion clearly and explained why it is time-critical.
Immediate ED attendance (999 if delay), escalation phrase, ring-ahead to the on-call team, nil by mouth.
Addressed the teenager’s embarrassment and autonomy, and confirmed transport.
Pain easing still means go, 999 if worse, teach-back of the plan, documented and hospital informed.

social.t: Shame about genital symptoms is a leading cause of late presentation in teenage boys. Normalise it and give him control over who is present.
Transport, care of other children or work commitments can stall an emergency transfer. Ask, and solve it during the call.

legal.t: A competent 15-year-old can consent to his own examination and treatment (Gillick competence), and his views should be respected. A parent can also consent on his behalf, and GMC 0–18 years allows urgent treatment to prevent serious harm in an emergency.
Record the time of onset, the advice given, the escalation phrase and that the family agreed to attend.

professional.t: GMC 0–18 years (2007, updated 2018): involve children and young people in decisions, communicate in a way they understand, and respect privacy.
When a telephone history fits an emergency, the safe action is direct transfer, not a face-to-face GP review. Ringing ahead supports continuity.

community.t: NHS information on testicular torsion; school nurse and youth health services for sexual health questions afterwards.

redFlags: Sudden severe testicular pain, especially with nausea or vomiting — emergency surgical assessment now
Groin or lower abdominal pain in a teenage boy — always ask about the testicle
Previous brief self-resolving episodes suggest intermittent torsion
psychosocial: Teenager’s embarrassment and reluctance to be examined
Parent’s wish not to “make a fuss”
Transport and anything that could stop them leaving now
ice: Idea: “a pulled muscle or a knock from football”
Concern: embarrassment and wasting hospital time
Expectation: advice to rest and take ibuprofen at home

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Suspected left testicular torsion: sudden severe testicular pain during exercise with vomiting in a 15-year-old, about 90 minutes from onset, with a possible previous brief episode. Needs immediate emergency surgical assessment.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The testicle hangs on a cord that carries its blood supply. Sometimes it twists, like a hosepipe kinking, and the blood can’t get through. Surgeons can untwist it, but only if they get to it quickly.”

management.reflectIce: “I know you both hoped it was a pulled muscle, and Kai, I know this is embarrassing. Going now is what protects you, and nobody at the hospital will think twice about it.”
management.psychosocial: Give Kai choices he controls; confirm transport and remove any barrier to leaving before ending the call.
sharedPlan: Immediate ED attendance by car now, or 999 if any delay or deterioration
Use the phrase “sudden severe testicular pain with vomiting, possible torsion”
Nil by mouth; GP rings ahead to the on-call team and documents
safetyNet: Pain easing does not mean it has resolved — still attend
999 if pain worsens, he becomes faint or unwell en route

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This is a time-critical station. The clinical decision is simple; candidates fail by taking too long to reach it, by being drawn into the pulled-muscle story, or by never winning over an embarrassed teenager.

items.fail: Offering a same-day GP appointment “so I can examine him”.
items.why: Examination cannot exclude torsion and the journey wastes time. Feedback: “management plan not appropriate to the urgency”.
items.fix: Send him straight to ED and ring ahead. Say why: “the surgeons are the ones who can check and fix this.”

items.fail: A full systematic history before reaching a decision at minute eight.
items.why: Poor prioritisation in an emergency is marked down in Tasks and Global Skills.
items.fix: Three questions — testicle, sudden onset, fever or urinary symptoms — then decide by minute three to five.

items.fail: Accepting the knock last week or the football as the explanation.
items.why: Exercise and minor trauma often precede torsion; an alternative story does not exclude it.
items.fix: “That may be part of it, but it doesn’t rule out a twist — only the hospital can.”

items.fail: Speaking only to the mother about Kai’s testicle while he listens.
items.why: Feedback: “did not involve the patient”. It deepens his embarrassment and resistance.
items.fix: Ask to speak to him, normalise it, and offer choices he controls.

items.fail: No nil-by-mouth advice, no escalation phrase, and no warning that easing pain still needs assessment.
items.why: Incomplete safety-netting is a standard failing statement in urgent-care stations.
items.fix: Nil by mouth, “possible torsion” at the desk, 999 if worse, and “if it eases, still go”.

items.fail: Ending the call without confirming they are actually leaving and how.
items.why: Feedback: “did not check understanding or agreement with the plan”.
items.fix: “Tell me what you’re doing now” — then end quickly so they can go.
